title: How World War II Reshaped the World

scenes.purpose: Hook: the war built today's world.

visual.title: One war, a new world
visual.statement: World War II did not just end in 1945. It built much of the world we still live in.

narration.text: In 1939, much of the world was ruled by European empires.
Barely ten years later, almost everything about how nations dealt with each other had changed.
Two superpowers faced each other across a divided Europe.
New institutions set rules for peace, trade and money.
And old empires were breaking apart into dozens of new nations.
To see why, start with the war itself.

scenes.purpose: Place the main events of the war in time.

events.label: Soviet Union invaded; Pearl Harbor attacked

narration.text: The war in Europe began on September 1, 1939, when Germany invaded Poland.
In 1941, Germany invaded the Soviet Union, and Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, pulling America in.
In June 1944, Allied troops landed in Normandy, opening a new front in the west.
Germany surrendered in May 1945.
Japan surrendered that August, after atomic bombs destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

scenes.purpose: Show who fought on each side.

narration.text: This was a truly global war.
On one side stood the Axis: Germany, Italy and Japan.
Against them were Britain and its empire, the United States, China and many others,
and the Soviet Union, which suffered the heaviest losses of all.
Fighting stretched from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and from North Africa to the Arctic.

scenes.purpose: Convey the human cost.

visual.title: The human cost

stats.label: people killed, at the lowest estimates

visual.note: Estimates of total deaths range from about 70 to 85 million.

narration.text: No war has ever killed so many people.
Somewhere between seventy and eighty-five million people died, most of them civilians.
That was about three percent of everyone alive in 1940.
Nazi Germany murdered six million Jews in the Holocaust.
The scale of that loss shaped every decision that followed.

scenes.purpose: Contrast the exhausted old powers with the two rising ones.

narration.text: When the guns fell silent, the old great powers were exhausted.
Much of Europe and Japan lay in ruins, their economies shattered.
Two countries emerged far stronger: the United States and the Soviet Union.
One was a capitalist democracy; the other, a communist state run by a single party.

scenes.purpose: Define superpower.

visual.title: A new kind of power
visual.definition: A state with the military, economic and political reach to shape events across the whole world.
visual.example: The word caught on in 1944, as the war's outcome became clear.

narration.text: A new word described them: superpower.
A superpower could shape events almost anywhere on Earth, with armies, money and ideas.
The term caught on in 1944, as it became clear who would win.

scenes.purpose: Hear the start of the Cold War in Churchill's words.

visual.title: An iron curtain
visual.quote: From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent.
visual.author: Winston Churchill

narration.text: The wartime allies soon became rivals.
In March 1946, Winston Churchill described a continent splitting in two.
From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent.
The phrase stuck, and so did the division.

scenes.purpose: Show the Cold War division of Europe.

narration.text: The line Churchill described ran from Stettin, on the Baltic Sea,
down to Trieste, on the Adriatic.
To the west, a military alliance called NATO formed in 1949.
To the east, the Soviet Union and its allies answered with the Warsaw Pact in 1955.
Germany itself was split in two, and Berlin became the front line of a Cold War.
That standoff would last more than forty years.

scenes.purpose: Introduce the goals of the postwar institutions.

visual.title: Never again
visual.statement: The victors tried to build institutions that would make another world war impossible.

narration.text: The victors were determined to prevent a third world war.
They built new institutions to keep the peace,
to steady the world economy,
and to protect the rights of every person.

scenes.purpose: Place the founding of the new institutions in time.

events.label: Bretton Woods creates the IMF and World Bank

narration.text: In July 1944, delegates from 44 countries met at Bretton Woods, in New Hampshire.
They created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.
In 1945, fifty nations signed the charter of the United Nations.
In 1946, the Nuremberg trials held Nazi leaders personally responsible for their crimes.
And in 1948, the UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

scenes.purpose: Explain how the Security Council and the veto work.

narration.text: At the heart of the UN sits the Security Council.
When a crisis threatens peace,
the Council debates a response.
But the five permanent members, the war's main victors, can each veto any decision.
If none does, the Council can order sanctions or even military action.
That veto still shapes world politics today.

scenes.purpose: Show the money behind the recovery.

stats.label: the gold price that anchored the dollar

narration.text: Money mattered as much as rules.
Under the Marshall Plan, America sent Western Europe more than thirteen billion dollars in aid.
And the Bretton Woods system tied currencies to the dollar, and the dollar to gold at thirty-five dollars an ounce.
The dollar became the world's main currency, and it still is.

scenes.purpose: Explain why empires began to fall.

visual.title: Empires begin to crumble
visual.statement: The war drained Europe's colonial powers and energized independence movements in Asia and Africa.
points: Europe too weak to hold on

narration.text: The war also cracked the foundations of the great European empires.
Britain, France and the Netherlands were too weak to hold their colonies by force for long.
Millions of colonial soldiers had fought for freedom abroad, and they wanted it at home.
And the new UN Charter spoke of the self-determination of peoples.

scenes.purpose: Place the main waves of independence in time.

narration.text: In 1947, India and Pakistan won independence from Britain.
In 1949, Indonesia won its freedom from the Netherlands.
In 1957, Ghana became one of the first African colonies to win independence.
And in 1960 alone, seventeen African nations became independent.

scenes.purpose: Show the Year of Africa on a map.

narration.text: Ghana's independence in 1957 inspired movements across the continent.
By the end of 1960, much of West and Central Africa had won its freedom.
That year became known as the Year of Africa.

scenes.purpose: Measure the change through UN membership.

stats.label: founding members of the UN in 1945

narration.text: You can measure the change at the United Nations.
It began with fifty-one members in 1945.
Today it has one hundred ninety-three, and most of them became independent after the war.

scenes.purpose: Define genocide and its origin.

visual.title: Naming a crime
visual.definition: Acts meant to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
visual.example: The lawyer Raphael Lemkin coined the word in 1944.

narration.text: The horror of the Holocaust forced the world to name a crime.
Genocide means acts meant to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
The lawyer Raphael Lemkin coined the word in 1944.
In 1948, the United Nations made genocide a crime under international law.

scenes.purpose: Show wartime technologies that changed peacetime.

visual.title: Science at war
visual.statement: Wartime research produced technologies that reshaped everyday life after 1945.

narration.text: The war also sped up science.
Radar and jet engines, rushed into service for battle, later transformed air travel.
Codebreakers and engineers built some of the first electronic computers.
And penicillin went from a laboratory curiosity to a mass-produced, life-saving drug.

scenes.purpose: Trace rockets from weapons to the space race.

narration.text: Rockets followed a similar path.
In 1944, a German V-2 missile became the first human-made object to reach space.
After the war, both superpowers recruited German rocket engineers.
Their rivalry produced ever larger missiles,
and those missiles launched the space race, from Sputnik to the Moon.

scenes.purpose: Explain the nuclear age.

visual.title: The nuclear age
visual.statement: Nuclear weapons made any direct war between the superpowers unthinkably dangerous.

narration.text: Above all, the war opened the nuclear age.
The superpowers raced to build ever more powerful bombs.
The fear of mutual destruction helped keep their rivalry from becoming a direct war.
And over time, it pushed them toward arms-control treaties.

scenes.purpose: Hear the founding idea of European integration.

visual.title: From enemies to partners
visual.quote: The solidarity in production thus established will make it plain that any war between France and Germany becomes not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible.
visual.author: Robert Schuman

narration.text: In Western Europe, old enemies chose a different path.
In 1950, French foreign minister Robert Schuman proposed pooling French and German coal and steel.
The solidarity in production thus established will make it plain that any war between France and Germany becomes not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible.
That plan grew, step by step, into today's European Union.

scenes.purpose: Trace the path to the European Union.

visual.title: From coal and steel to the EU

events.label: Treaty of Rome creates a common market

narration.text: In 1951, six countries formed the European Coal and Steel Community.
In 1957, the Treaty of Rome created a common market.
And in 1993, the European Union was born.

scenes.purpose: Contrast the world before and after the war.

narration.text: Step back, and the change is striking.
Before the war, empires ruled much of the globe, and Europe sat at its center.
After it, new nations, two superpowers and a web of global institutions took their place.

scenes.purpose: Close with the war's lasting legacy.

visual.title: Still living in 1945's world
visual.statement: The UN, the dollar's global role and many borders on today's map trace back to the war.

narration.text: The Cold War ended in 1991, but much of the postwar order is still with us.
The UN, the global role of the dollar and many modern borders all trace back to those years.
The war ended long ago, but in many ways, we still live in the world it built.
